title: Ember InsurTech throughput & latency scan — hybrid POC notes
content:
Executive summary:

This note captures the end-to-end benchmarking we ran for Ember InsurTech during the hybrid POC (hosted + dedicated fallback) on 2027-10-12 → 2027-10-19. Goal: validate that the proposed routing policy (hosted primary, dedicated for burst and privacy-sensitive requests) meets Ember’s latency SLOs (p95 < 300ms for interactive prompts, sustain 500 tps for batch inference) while keeping steady-state unit cost below Ember’s target ($0.45 per 1k output tokens equivalent).

Key takeaways (short):
- Baseline (hosted Redwood-Medium-v2 on H100): interactive p50=34ms, p95=220ms, p99=470ms at 120 tps.
- Dedicated A100 pool (quantized LlamaX-30B-4bit) used as a cost buffer: p50=48ms, p95=360ms, p99=820ms at 400 tps; cost per 1M tokens ~ $150 (after reserved commitment amortization).
- KV prefix caching reduced average token compute by ~28% for templated workflows (policy-lookup flows), improving p95 by ~18% under the same concurrency.
- Coldstart behavior for private on-prem nodes: first 30s spike added 850–1,200ms to tail latency; warm steady-state saw acceptable numbers.

Test matrix and rationale:
- Models tested: Redwood-Medium-v2 (8B FP16), Redwood-Large-v1 (30B FP16), LlamaX-30B-4bit (quantized, dedicated-only).
- Hardware: hosted H100 80GB (shared), dedicated A100 80GB pooled (reserved capacity), on-prem rack with 2xH100 (customer air-gapped test harness).
- Workloads: (A) interactive short prompts (avg 80 tokens output), 10–200 concurrent users; (B) high-throughput batch routing (large BATCH size 256 requests), 500–1,000 concurrent streams; (C) mixed hybrid: 80% templated prompts (high cache hit), 20% ad-hoc.
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p95/p99 generation latencies, throughput (requests/sec and tokens/sec), GPU utilization, memory/KV cache hit rate, and effective cost per 1M output tokens (inc. commit amortization for reserved capacity).

Environment and config notes:
- Serving runtime: Redwood unified runtime with continuous batching and KV caching enabled for all runs.
- Batching: default dynamic batching window 20ms, max batch size 512 for A100, 256 for H100.
- KV cache: prefix cache seeded using 10k templated prompts from Ember test corpus. Cache TTL 10 minutes during experiments.
- Autoscale policy on Dedicated: reactive with target GPU util 65%, scale-up cooldown 45s, scale-down 3m.
- Routing: hosted primary via weighted policy; when hosted 5xx rate > 0.5% or queue depth > 100, traffic moved to dedicated pool with warmup concurrency.
- Measurement tooling: internal load harness (github:repo/ember-poc#45) + Prometheus scrape + custom cost calculator for reserved commitments.

Results — interactive workload (avg 80 tokens):
- Redwood-Medium-v2 @ Hosted H100 (shared):
  - concurrency sweep 10 -> 200 users
  - peak steady at 120 tps: p50 34ms, p90 160ms, p95 220ms, p99 470ms
  - throughput plateau observed at ~180 tps; beyond that p99 rapidly grows > 1.2s due to queueing + token generation backpressure.
  - cost estimate: $0.38 per 1k output tokens (hosted price model used).

- LlamaX-30B-4bit @ Dedicated A100 pool (quantized):
  - optimized for throughput, sustained 400 tps with p50 48ms, p90 240ms, p95 360ms, p99 820ms (under 400 tps stress).
  - coldstart + model swap penalty when autoscale added nodes mid-test: observed 700–1,100ms tail spikes for first request routed to new node.
  - cost estimate (incl reserved amortization): ~ $0.15 per 1k output tokens if commitment >= 3 months; spot/overage pricing increases effective cost to $0.22 per 1k tokens.

- Redwood-Large-v1 @ Hosted H100 (FP16, larger context):
  - best quality, higher compute: p50 65ms, p95 420ms at 80 tps; beyond 90 tps latency escalates.
  - cost estimate: $0.92 per 1k output tokens.

Results — batch and throughput workload (BATCH=256):
- Dedicated A100 cluster achieved sustained 1,000 requests/min for 10k-token batches (throughput bound by GPU memory and batching window).
- Effective tokens/sec peaked at 85k tokens/sec on 4 A100s with quantized LlamaX; p95 per-request latency remained under 1.6s for large batches.
- Hosted runs hit concurrency limits earlier due to multi-tenant throttling; tail latencies were less predictable under large batch workloads.

KV cache impact (templated flows):
- Cache hit rate: 62% on templated corpus (10k seed phrases).
- When hit: per-request compute reduced ~28%, p95 down by ~18% vs no-cache baseline on hosted runs.
- Miss penalty: 1.0–1.6x extra latency depending on model size (larger models suffer more).

Observed anomalies and root cause hypotheses:
1) P99 microbursts on dedicated pool correlated with node rebalancing during scale-down. Hypothesis: our scale-down cooldown and in-flight request draining policy causes transient queue spikes.
2) On-prem coldstart penalty larger than hosted because the on-prem image initialization pulls large model artifacts sequentially from local NFS; parallel prefetch would reduce this.
3) A small set (~0.7%) of templated prompts caused repeated cache churn due to near-duplicates with differing trailing punctuation — suggests normalization pre-cache would improve effective hit rate.

Cost sensitivity and breakeven analysis (customer targets):
- Ember target: <= $0.45 per 1k output tokens while meeting p95 < 300ms interactive.
- Our blended recommendation: primary hosted Redwood-Medium-v2 for interactive, overflow and privacy-sensitive routing to dedicated LlamaX-30B-4bit.
  - Blended steady-state cost estimate: $0.31 per 1k tokens (70% hosted / 30% dedicated), p95 ~ 235ms.
  - If Ember increases templated cache hit to 80% (improvements in prompt normalization), cost drops to ~ $0.24 per 1k tokens and p95 to ~200ms.
- Breakeven point vs all-hosted Redwood-Large: moving 40% traffic to dedicated quantized LlamaX meets cost target while quality loss acceptable on 30% of requests (lower-criticality workflows).

Recommendations (actionable):
1) Implement prompt normalization and punctuation de-duplication before caching to boost KV hit rate — target 75–80% hit.
2) Adjust dedicated autoscale: increase scale-up aggressiveness (cooldown 20–30s) and heighten scale-down timeout to 6m to avoid rebalancing microbursts.
3) Pre-warm quantized models on dedicated nodes during predicted traffic windows using warmup cadence (deploy hook) to reduce coldstart tail.
4) Use hosted Redwood-Medium-v2 for low-latency interactive flows, route high-volume templated queries to dedicated pool with aggressive caching.
5) For privacy-sensitive flows, prefer dedicated pool but enable short-lived prefix cache eviction to comply with retention policy.

Risks and trade-offs:
- Quality: quantized LlamaX shows small quality regressions in rare edge-case completions vs Redwood-Large; Ember product team should validate on their eval set for business-critical flows.
- Operational: reserved commitments reduce unit cost but introduce utilization risk; recommend 3-month pilot reserved commit sized at 40–60% of expected peak burst.

Next steps and owners:
- Prompt normalization prototype (Asha) — deliver sample preprocessor and analyze new cache hit rate by 2027-10-28.
- Autoscale policy tweak and re-run stress sweep (Owen) — target 2027-11-03.
- Customer quality evaluation on Ember policy dataset for quantized LlamaX (Marco) — target 2027-10-30.
- Prepare short one-pager for Ember execs summarizing cost/latency trade-offs and recommended contract sizes (Asha + Solutions Eng) — 2027-11-01.

Appendix — raw numbers (selected):
- Hosted Redwood-Medium-v2 (H100) @ 120 tps: mean token time 11.6ms, generation tokens/sec ~ 9.6k, GPU util 64%.
- Dedicated LlamaX-30B-4bit (A100) @ 400 tps: mean token time 6.1ms, generation tokens/sec ~ 28.4k, GPU util 72%.
- KV cache: hit=62%, miss latency delta +140ms (median).
- Coldstart on-prem: 850–1,200ms extra for first request; subsequent requests within 60s returned to baseline.

Notes and hints for follow-up measurement runs:
- When measuring tail latency, include workload jitter to emulate real traffic (Poisson arrival process); synthetic steady streams under-estimate p99 behavior.
- Capture model swap events and label traces with node id to correlate rebalancing with latency spikes.
- Run mixed workload tests during host maintenance windows to observe multi-tenant interference margins.

End of note.

Attachments (local):
- load-harness-results-2027-10-19.csv (raw),
- plot-p95-vs-concurrency.png (scatter),

Comments welcome — especially from Ember folks on tolerable quality delta vs cost gains.
